title: EXISTS Operator
description: Learn how to use the SQL Server EXISTS operator to test for the existence of rows in a subquery.

data.text: The EXISTS operator is a logical operator that checks whether a subquery returns any rows. It returns TRUE if the subquery returns one or more rows, and FALSE otherwise. EXISTS is useful for testing the existence of related data without returning the actual data.

data.title: EXISTS Syntax
data.content: Tests whether the subquery returns any rows.

data.text: The subquery in an EXISTS clause must be a SELECT statement. As soon as the subquery returns at least one row, EXISTS returns TRUE and stops processing immediately. Even if the subquery returns NULL, EXISTS evaluates to TRUE.
The following example returns all rows from the customers table because the subquery SELECT NULL always returns a row.

data.title: EXISTS with SELECT NULL
data.content: Returns all customers because the subquery always produces a row.
data.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers
WHERE
    EXISTS (SELECT NULL)
ORDER BY
    first_name,
    last_name;

data.alt: SQL Server EXISTS with NULL example output

data.text: The following query finds customers who have placed more than two orders. The correlated subquery counts orders for each customer and checks if the count exceeds two.

data.title: EXISTS with Correlated Subquery
data.content: Finds customers with more than two orders using a correlated subquery.
data.code:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    first_name,
    last_name
FROM
    sales.customers c
WHERE
    EXISTS (
        SELECT
            COUNT(*)
        FROM
            sales.orders o
        WHERE
            customer_id = c.customer_id
        GROUP BY
            customer_id
        HAVING
            COUNT(*) > 2
    )
ORDER BY
    first_name,
    last_name;

data.alt: SQL Server EXISTS with correlated subquery example output

data.text: The following two queries return the same result — orders placed by customers from San Jose. The first uses IN, and the second uses EXISTS.

data.title: IN vs EXISTS
data.content: Comparing IN and EXISTS for the same query.
data.code:
-- Using IN
SELECT *
FROM sales.orders
WHERE customer_id IN (
    SELECT customer_id
    FROM sales.customers
    WHERE city = 'San Jose'
)
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;

-- Using EXISTS
SELECT *
FROM sales.orders o
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT customer_id
    FROM sales.customers c
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND city = 'San Jose'
)
ORDER BY o.customer_id, o.order_date;

data.alt: SQL Server EXISTS vs IN example output

data.text: EXISTS returns TRUE or FALSE and short-circuits as soon as a matching row is found. JOIN extends the result set by combining columns from related tables. Use EXISTS when you need to check for the existence of related rows without returning their data.

data.title: EXISTS Key Points
points: EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns any rows.
It short-circuits as soon as the first matching row is found.
EXISTS is often more efficient than IN for correlated subqueries.
Use EXISTS to check for the existence of related data without returning it.
